## Your risks

What could reach a household like yours in Coos County, Oregon over the next 10 years: the likeliest events, and the rarer ones that can kill, most likely first.

### What to know and do

#### 1. Strong wind

Nearly every household like yours will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years (about 1.1 times a year).[10, 15]

**Includes:** derecho.

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best.[16] The next best is a small, windowless room or basement on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.[16, 17] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[16] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[18]

**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[16] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[18]

**How bad:** Minor (rough data).

#### 2. Medical emergency

Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.[19, 20]

**Includes:** far from emergency care; falls.

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[21] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[22] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[23] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[24] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[25]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[26] Do not use expired medicines.[27]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 3. Heat wave

Of 100 households like yours, about 95 will go through a heat wave in the next ten years.[15]

**Includes:** a blackout during a heat wave.

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[28] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[29] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[29] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[28] In a drought, follow local limits on water use, and make saving water a daily habit.[30]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[28] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[29] Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature of 103°F or more, hot, red skin that may be dry or damp, a fast, strong pulse, confusion or passing out. Call 911, move the person somewhere cooler, cool them with cool cloths or a cool bath, and give them nothing to drink.[31]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 4. Burst pipe or water leak

Of 100 households like yours, about 14 will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.[32]

**Includes:** sewer backup.

**What helps.** Find your main water shut-off valve now, and show everyone how to turn it off. A burst pipe can flood a room quickly.[33, 34] Once a year, check the hoses to the water heater, washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, and replace any that crack or leak. A leak alarm can warn you early.[33] In freezing weather, let a faucet drip at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher.[34] Home and renters policies usually cover burst pipes. Many do not cover a sewer backup unless you add that cover, and floods need their own policy.[33]

**What to avoid.** Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame; use a hair dryer. Watch for electric shock around standing water.[34] Do not leave home while the washing machine or dishwasher is running.[33]

**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).

#### 5. Earthquake

Of 100 households like yours, about 11 will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.[9, 35]

**Includes:** liquefaction; fire after an earthquake.

**What helps.** Practice Drop, Cover and Hold On: drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.[14] Secure bookcases, water heaters, TVs and other heavy things, and keep heavy objects on low shelves. A standard homeowner's policy does not cover earthquake damage.[14] Store water in case the taps stop. On the coast, the shaking is your warning. As soon as it stops, walk to high ground or inland without waiting for an alert.[4, 36] A loud roar from the ocean, or water that suddenly drains away, is another sign.[37]

**What to avoid.** Do not run outside during shaking, and stay away from doorways.[14] Do not go back to the shore until officials say it is safe. Tsunami waves can keep coming for hours.[4]

**How bad:** Very severe (mostly data).

#### 6. Tsunami

Of 100 households like yours, about 9 (3–18) will have to leave home or work for a tsunami warning in the next ten years.[7, 9, 10]

**What helps.** The steps under "Earthquake" above apply here too.

**How bad:** Severe (rough data).

#### 7. Flooding from rivers or heavy rain

Of 100 households like yours, about 4 (1–10) will have flood water reach their home in the next ten years.[8, 10]

**Includes:** flash flood; basement or street flooding in heavy rain.

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[38] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[38] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[39] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[38]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[38] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[40] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[38] Leave if you are told to.[41]

**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).

#### 8. House fire

Of 100 households like yours, about 3 will have a house fire in the next ten years.[11]

**Includes:** carbon monoxide poisoning; lithium battery fire.

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[42] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[43] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[43] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[43] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[43] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[44]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[43] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[43] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[43]

**How bad:** Severe (based on data).

- These chances are for Coos County as a whole. A home near a river, the coast or a steep slope can face more; the county's average is what the plan uses.
- Ambulances take longer to reach rural homes, so first-aid skills and supplies count for more here.
- Heat waves are marked Serious for this household because the home has no air conditioning; they are most dangerous for households like yours.

## Your targets

How long to be ready for each kind of disruption at the 1-in-500 setting. At this setting, about 2 in 100 households like yours will face a longer disruption of any one kind in the next 10 years; about 3 in 100 will face at least one kind that runs past its target. That is why the plan also gives you ways to cope when a target runs out.[10, 88]

| If this happens | Be ready for | Help likely in | Mostly back in | Enough at |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No grid power at home | about 6 months (2 months to 1 year) | about 2 weeks | about 6 months | six months |
| Tap water must be treated | not needed at this setting | not known | not known | free steps |
| No tap water at all | about 1 year (6 months to 1 year) | about 2 weeks | about 9 months | one year |
| Can't get to a store | about 2 months (1½–6) | about 2 weeks | about 3 years | three months |
| Dangerous heat or cold indoors | about 2 weeks (10 days to 2 weeks) | about 3 days | about 5 days | two weeks |

| No phone, internet or card payments | about 1½ months (3 weeks to 3 months) | not known | not known | three months |

Brackets show how uncertain a target is. "Not known": no restoration records for the event behind that target.

**How well do these numbers hold up?** Tested against 22 real disasters, this version covered 6, partly covered 9, fell short on 6 and could not model 1.[89] Treat each target as a floor, not a promise. If your area has lived through something longer, plan for that.

### No grid power at home: about 6 months (2 months to 1 year)

**What helps.** A light for each person, a radio and phone power are in your plan; keeping food cold and charging up are on the forecast list; registries are under Local help.

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[90] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[91] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone outside to fresh air, then call 911.[92] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[91] Treat every downed power line as live: stay at least 35 feet from it and anything it touches, and call 911.[93, 94] If one falls on your car, stay inside unless the car is on fire.[95]

The worst power cut in your region's records (where it was worst, about 147 miles (237 km) away) was power cut, cause not recorded, February 2021; being ready for 6 months would have outlasted it for at least 9 in 10 of the homes that lost power.[9, 78, 96, 97, 98]

### No tap water at all: about 1 year (6 months to 1 year)

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[99] You can pick a level in the plan. About 3 liters a day covers drinking to survive, one gallon is the basic default, and about 4 gallons (15 liters) is the humanitarian minimum for drinking, cooking and washing.[100] A tank water heater holds 20 to 80 gallons of clean water.[101, 102] For long outages, a filter and a source of raw water go further than more jugs.[88] Filters do not remove viruses, so add a disinfectant such as chlorine dioxide after filtering.[103] A two-bucket toilet keeps waste safe when toilets cannot flush.[104]

**What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[99] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[105] Never drink pool or spa water. Use it only for washing and cleaning.[102] After a flood, do not drink from a private well until it has been disinfected and tested. Your health department can tell you how.[106]

This rounds up to a year: before rounding it is about 7 months, just past 6 months.[7, 9, 10, 96, 97, 98]

### Can't get to a store: about 2 months (1½–6)

**What to avoid.** Do not buy everything at once. It strains your budget and the store. Do not buy or eat from cans that bulge, leak, are rusted or are deeply dented.[107] Do not trust a kit's "days" label. Check the calories on the package instead.

### Dangerous heat or cold indoors: about 2 weeks (10 days to 2 weeks)

**What helps.** Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone.[28, 108] In heat, go where there is air conditioning. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[28] Cover windows with drapes or shades.[29] In cold, close off rooms you don't need, stuff towels under doors, and cover windows with blankets at night. Have extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats.[108] Babies under one year old should never sleep in a cold room.[108] If you cannot keep your home warm, go to a warming center. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[109] If you heat with wood, have the stove and chimney professionally inspected and cleaned every year, because creosote from the smoke builds up and can start a fire.[110]

**What to avoid.** Fans move air but do not lower body temperature.[29] Above 90°F indoors, a fan can make you hotter.[28] Never heat your home with a gas oven, and never use a grill or camp stove indoors.[90] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning: get outside, then call 911.[92] Keep space heaters 3 feet from anything that can burn.[111] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[29]

**What helps.** See Medicine under Special needs.

**What to avoid.** Do not use expired medicines. Weak antibiotics can fail to treat an infection.[27] Do not share antibiotics or save them for later.[26]

**What helps.** See Your family plan and Your shelter plan.

**What to avoid.** Many people wait to check with others before they act on a warning.[112] Always follow the instructions of local officials, and leave early enough to avoid being trapped by bad weather.[2] Never walk or drive through floodwater. Six inches of moving water can knock you down.[38]

**What helps.** See Your family plan and Your shelter plan.

**What to avoid.** Do not force down water when you are not thirsty. Too much water can be harmful.[113] In heat, do not drink more than 6 cups an hour.[114] If you are stuck in a car in a snowstorm, staying in the car is often safest. **What helps.** See "Medical emergency" under Your risks.

**What helps.** See "House fire" under Your risks and the safety rules under Your plan.

**What to avoid.** If a person or pet is still inside, get out, call 911, and tell firefighters where they are.[43] Never heat your home with an oven.[111] Turn off space heaters when you leave the room or go to bed.[111] Replace 9-volt alarm batteries at least once a year.[42] If you smell gas or hear hissing, get everyone out without touching switches or phones, then call 911 and the gas company from a safe distance.[115, 116] Only a professional should turn the gas back on.[116]

## Your shelter plan

Pick a spot for each danger below, at home and at work, and practice going there.[12]

**Strong wind.** In a high wind or severe thunderstorm warning, go inside a sturdy building, to an inside room or basement.[127] Stay away from windows while damaging wind is near.[128]

**Earthquake.** Drop where you are, cover your head and neck, and hold on. Crawl under a sturdy table, or next to an inside wall away from windows. Do not run outside.[14]

**Chemical release.** If told to stay inside, go to an above-ground room with few openings. Close the windows, doors and vents, turn off fans and air conditioning, and seal the room with plastic sheeting and duct tape.[129]

**Smoke.** Make one room a clean room: close its windows and doors, and run an air cleaner that does not make ozone.[119]

**Radiation.** If officials warn of fallout, get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Go to a basement or the middle of a brick or concrete building.[85]

## When a storm, freeze or heat wave is forecast

Hurricanes, winter storms and heat waves usually come with warning. Keep your phone charged when one is forecast, and use the time the same way each time.[3]

**Before any storm**

- Charge phones, power banks and other batteries.[130] 
- Fill the car's tank and get some cash, since card readers and cash machines need power.[130] If you would leave in an electric car, charge it fully.[131]
- Refill prescriptions if you can.[130]
- Fill the bathtub and other large containers with water for flushing and cleaning.[130]
- Turn the fridge to its coldest setting and keep the doors shut.[130] A full freezer keeps food cold for about 48 hours, a fridge for about four.[91]
- Bring in or tie down outdoor furniture and grills.[3]
- Check your evacuation zone and your plan to leave.[3]
- Check with neighbors, older adults and anyone who may need help.[3]

**Before a hard freeze.** Let hot and cold water drip from a faucet at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher. Make sure everyone knows how to shut off the water in case a pipe bursts.[34]

**Before a heat wave.** Pick a place to cool down, such as a library, or ask your local health department about cooling options. Plan to check on family, older adults and neighbors. Fans do not lower body temperature.[29]

## After a disaster: the first 30 days

**Your county.** Coos County, Oregon had 2 federal major-disaster declarations in the last five full years.[155]

Recovery takes weeks. These steps come in rough order.

**Going home.** Go back only when local officials say it is safe. Do not go inside if you smell gas or the building looks damaged.[156] Run a generator only outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[90]

**Insurance and records.** Before you clean up, take photos and videos and make a list of the damage.[156] Keep every receipt.[157] Call your insurer as soon as you can, and an adjuster will come to inspect. Check the adjuster's estimate, and talk to them before you sign a repair contract.[158]

**Help from FEMA.** If a federal disaster declaration covers your county, apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.[159] FEMA help does not replace insurance.[160]

**Scams.** FEMA never charges to apply or to inspect.[161] Its inspectors carry an official photo ID and never ask for your bank details; a FEMA shirt is not an ID.[157] Never sign your insurance check over to a contractor, and walk away from anyone who wants cash up front.[162]

**Medicine.** In a declared disaster, Medicare drug plans can help you find a pharmacy and replace lost medicine.[163] Many states let a pharmacist give an emergency supply when your prescriber cannot be reached, and the rules differ by state.[142] Healthcare Ready's Rx Open map shows which pharmacies are open in a disaster area.[164]

**Papers.** To replace lost IDs, start with your birth certificate, from the vital records office of the state where you were born.[165]

**How likely here.** From your own power curve, power out for two months or more: between 1 in 49 and 1 in 10 households like yours in the next 10 years; for three months or more: between 1 in 120 and 1 in 11.[9, 78, 96, 97, 98]

These pointers are for the rare event that lasts for months. They are places to start, not a manual.

**Rain.** Each state sets its own rules on collecting rain, and the rules vary widely, so check yours.[166] Rainwater is not safe to drink until germs and chemicals are removed, but it can water plants you do not eat.[167]

**Wells.** A well pump stops when the power goes out. Have a licensed electrician connect any generator.[168] A hand pump fitted to the well can still draw water in a long outage; test and treat that water before drinking it.[169]

**Fuel.** Stored fuel does not keep forever, so use it and replace it. Following the International Fire Code, one Utah fire department limits gasoline at home to 25 gallons in approved containers, with no more than 10 in an attached garage and none in a basement. Ask your local fire department for your rules.[170]

**Toilets.** After a strong earthquake, toilets may not flush for weeks or months. A twin-bucket toilet keeps pee and poo apart, and handling poo safely stops diseases like cholera.[104]

**Food.** Badly home-canned food can cause botulism. Vegetables, meat and fish need a pressure canner.[171] Use tested recipes, such as those from the National Center for Home Food Preservation.[172] Your state or county Extension service can help with growing and preserving food.[171]

**Spirits.** Keep regular sleep and wake times, take breaks from the news, and talk with people you trust.[173] Keep books, games and puzzles for children.[135]
